items.question: How does splitting a payment avoid MDR?
items.answer: UPI MDR applies only above ₹2,000 per transaction, and then to the full amount rather than just the excess. A ₹7,500 collection taken as one payment crosses that line and is charged on the whole ₹7,500, but taken as four QR codes of ₹2,000 or less, every transaction sits under the threshold and nothing is charged.

items.question: Why is the default ₹1,999 and not ₹2,000?
items.answer: ₹2,000 is the boundary itself. Setting the ceiling one rupee below it keeps every transaction clearly under the threshold rather than exactly on it, which avoids any argument about how a particular acquirer rounds or interprets the limit. You can change the figure if you prefer.

items.question: Is my UPI ID sent to Setu's servers?

items.question: Do UPI payments from a bank account have MDR anyway?
items.answer: Up to ₹2,000, no. From 15 October 2026, UPI merchant payments above ₹2,000 carry 0.4% MDR on the full transaction value, capped at ₹300. RuPay debit and UPI Autopay mandates stay exempt, and so do merchants receiving under ₹1 lakh a month through UPI QR — so check whether the charge applies to you before splitting anything.

items.question: Is it allowed to split a payment this way?
items.answer: Collecting several separate payments from a customer is ordinary commercial practice, and nothing here bypasses a payment system's controls. That said, acquirer agreements differ, and some prohibit deliberately structuring transactions to avoid fees. Check your own merchant agreement before making this a routine practice.

body.headline: Why this works

body.headline: What is a quotation?
paragraphs: A quotation, also called a quote or estimate, is the priced offer you send before a customer commits: what you will supply, at what rate, with what tax, and how long the price holds. It lets the customer compare, negotiate and approve, and once accepted it becomes the basis for the sales order or invoice. This quotation generator puts that offer on a clean page with a validity date, so a rate you gave in June is not held against you in September.

No tax is payable on a quote itself, but it should still show GST line by line. A registered business customer usually compares your pre-tax price because they can claim [input tax credit](/glossary/input-tax-credit), while a consumer cares about the all-in figure. GST rates were rationalised from 22 September 2025, mostly into 5% and 18% slabs, so check the tax % on any old quote template or price list before you reuse it, and quote the rate that applies on the date of the quote.

The words get used loosely, but there is a useful difference. An estimate is an approximate figure that may change once the job is clear, as with repairs or interiors. A quotation is a firm price for the validity period. A [proforma invoice](/glossary/proforma-invoice), sometimes called a proforma quote, is often sent once the customer agrees, laid out like a bill so they can pay an advance or get internal approval. Use the word that matches what you are promising.

body.headline: What is a receipt generator?
paragraphs: A receipt is the customer's record of a sale: who sold, what was bought, how much it cost, when, and how it was settled, whether in cash, by UPI, by card or on credit (udhaar). Handing one over with every sale settles most "I already paid" disputes and makes returns easier to check. A receipt generator lets you set the look once, with logo, header, footer and paper size, and then print a receipt for any sale in that same format.

Printing your GSTIN on a receipt does not turn it into a GST [tax invoice](/glossary/tax-invoice). A tax invoice needs more, such as the taxable value, the GST rate and the CGST, SGST or IGST amounts, plus HSN or SAC codes where they apply, and this receipt does not calculate tax. If you are GST-registered, treat it as a payment slip, not a replacement for the tax invoice or bill of supply your sales need. When a business customer wants a bill to claim input tax credit, issue one from the [Invoice Generator](/tools/invoice-generator).

Most counters print on 80 mm or 58 mm thermal rolls. The 80 mm width leaves room for longer item names and is common on desktop receipt printers, while 58 mm is typical of small and portable printers. A4 suits shops that bill on an ordinary office printer. Thermal paper fades with heat and time, so keep your own record of each sale rather than relying on the customer's copy.

body.headline: What is a barcode generator?
paragraphs: A barcode stores a product code as bars that a scanner reads in a fraction of a second, so the person at the counter types nothing and bills the right item. A barcode generator turns a code you already have, such as an [SKU](/glossary/sku), an item number or a GTIN, into a printable image. The bars hold only the code. The name and price live in your billing software, which looks the code up when it is scanned, so the same barcode keeps working when you change the price.

Which type you choose depends on who will scan it. EAN-13 is the 13-digit number on packaged goods. If your product will be sold through supermarkets, distributors or online marketplaces, that number should be a [GTIN](/glossary/gtin) licensed to your company by GS1 India, and Indian numbers usually begin with 890. A made-up EAN-13 can clash with a real product elsewhere. For codes that only your own shop scans, Code 128 is simpler: it takes letters and numbers, so an SKU like RICE-5KG works as it is.

QR codes work differently. They are square, hold far more data than a line barcode and are usually scanned with a phone camera, which suits a web link, a menu or a UPI payment link printed on a counter card. Many basic counter scanners read only line barcodes, so for billing products keep to EAN-13 or Code 128, and use QR for what customers scan with their own phones.

body.headline: What is a price label printer?
paragraphs: A price label tells the customer what an item costs before they have to ask, and with a barcode on it, the counter can bill the item with one scan. Shops use them on loose and unbranded goods such as hardware, stationery, garments and gift items, and on shelf edges where many identical items sit together. A price label printer lays out the name, price and barcode for each product and sends the whole batch to your printer.

There are two common kinds of label stock. A4 sheets of sticky labels work with the inkjet or laser printer you already have and suit occasional batches. Rolls for a [thermal printer](/glossary/thermal-printer) need no ink or toner and print one label at a time, which suits shops that label new stock every day. Direct thermal labels can fade with heat and sunlight over time, so they are better for price stickers than for anything that must last for years.

One rule to keep in mind: for pre-packaged goods, the [MRP](/glossary/mrp) and the other declarations required under Legal Metrology rules belong on the pack itself, and goods cannot be sold above the printed MRP. Your own price sticker is for your counter and your customers' convenience; it does not replace those declarations and should never show more than the MRP on the pack. If you pack goods in advance yourself, such as dry fruits in sealed packets, check whether those packs need the declarations too.

body.headline: What is a stock register?
paragraphs: A stock register, also called an inventory register, is a running record of every item you keep for sale: what came in, what went out and what is left. Each entry ties a quantity to a date and a reason, such as a supplier delivery, a sale, a customer return or breakage, so the closing figure can always be traced back. For a kirana shop, a medical store or a restaurant store room, it answers the daily question of what to reorder and the monthly one of where stock went missing.

In India the register also feeds your books. Your CA/CPA needs the [closing stock](/glossary/closing-stock) figure at the end of the financial year to finalise the profit and loss account and balance sheet, and dated movements make that figure easier to defend if it is questioned in an audit. GST rules also expect registered businesses, other than composition dealers, to keep stock accounts of goods received and supplied, including goods lost, stolen, destroyed, written off or given away as free samples, which is what a stock in and out register records.

Setu's Stock Register works on the same products as the free [Browser Based POS](/products/browser-based-pos). For products with stock tracking switched on, counter sales are deducted automatically, so you only record what the till cannot see: deliveries, damaged packs, free samples and corrections after a physical count. That keeps the register short enough to maintain on a busy day, without a second copy of your stock list in a notebook or a spreadsheet.

body.headline: What is a purchase register?
paragraphs: A purchase register is a date-wise record of every bill you receive from suppliers: who you bought from, the bill number, what you bought, what it cost and how you paid. It answers everyday questions quickly. How much did we buy from this wholesaler last month? Was that bill paid in cash, or is it still on credit? For a shop, pharmacy or restaurant it is also where stock control starts, because what you buy is what should be on the shelf or in the kitchen.

Under GST, registered businesses have to keep accounts of their inward supplies, and the purchase register is the list your CA/CPA works from when matching supplier bills with [GSTR-2B](/glossary/gstr-2b) before claiming [input tax credit](/glossary/input-tax-credit). A bill missing from the register is easy to overlook at return time, and a bill entered twice can overstate both your costs and the credit you think you are owed.

Kept up to date, a purchase register also shows how you buy. You can see which supplier you depend on most, how often you restock a fast-moving item and whether the unit cost of your key products is creeping up. That is the information you want in hand before you negotiate rates, switch suppliers or decide how much to order next time.

items.answer: No. The GSTIN field accepts whatever you type and does not check the format or look the number up. Confirm it on the GST portal's Search Taxpayer page before saving. items.answer: The supplier book is your list of vendors and their details, and it changes only when a supplier's details change. body.headline: What is a supplier book (vendor register)?
paragraphs: A **supplier book**, or vendor register, is the master list of everyone you buy from: their phone, email, billing address, GSTIN and anything you have agreed with them. It holds no bills or amounts. It is the reference that your purchase entries, orders and payments draw on. When the details live in one place, you stop typing the same supplier's name three different ways, purchase bills match the right vendor, and a new staff member can call the right person for a re-order without searching old WhatsApp chats.

For a GST-registered business, the supplier's [GSTIN](/glossary/gstin) is the field that matters most. Input tax credit on a purchase reaches you only when the supplier reports that invoice against your GSTIN, after which it shows up in your [GSTR-2B](/glossary/gstr-2b). Keeping each supplier's correct GSTIN on file makes the monthly match of purchase bills against GSTR-2B quicker and helps you spot the supplier who has not filed. The first two digits of a GSTIN are the state code. If a supplier's code differs from yours, their bills will usually carry IGST rather than CGST plus SGST.

body.headline: What is a business expense tracker?
paragraphs: An **expense tracker** is the digital form of the kharcha register many shops keep at the counter: a dated list of what the business spends on rent, salaries, electricity, transport, repairs, marketing and purchases. Each entry notes the date, category, amount, how it was paid and what it was for. Totalled by month and category, the register shows your running costs at a glance and gives you most of the figures for the [operating expenses](/glossary/operating-expense) section of your profit and loss account.

Expenses are where small-business profit quietly leaks. Cash paid to a plumber, a UPI transfer for diesel or a tea-and-snacks bill rarely reaches the books unless someone writes it down the same day. A monthly expense register lets you compare months, spot a bill that keeps creeping up, and hand your accountant one file instead of a bag of receipts. Keep the original bills and GST invoices as well, because your CA/CPA needs them to support the entries and to claim [input tax credit](/glossary/input-tax-credit) where it is allowed.

Recording the payment mode pays off later. When each entry says cash, UPI, card or bank transfer, matching expenses against your bank statement and cash book takes minutes, and you can see how much of your spending still goes out in cash. That matters at tax time too: income tax rules generally disallow a business deduction for a cash payment above ₹10,000 to one person in a day, so large bills are better paid by UPI or bank transfer.

body.headline: What is a cash book?
paragraphs: A cash book is the daily register of every rupee that comes into and goes out of the cash drawer, kept in date order with a running balance. Many shops know it as the rokad bahi or rojnamcha: cash sales collected on one side, payments for tea, transport, wages and small purchases on the other, and the day's closing balance carried forward as the next morning's opening. It is the simplest of the [books of accounts](/glossary/books-of-accounts) and often the first one a business keeps.

Cash is the asset that goes missing most easily. When the closing balance in the book is compared with the notes and coins actually in the drawer each evening, a shortfall shows up the same day, while the person on the counter still remembers what happened. A cash book also gives your CA/CPA a record that supports cash sales and cash expenses at year-end, and it supplies the cash figure your balance sheet and cash flow statement need.

Cash still pays for many small daily expenses in Indian shops, but income tax rules restrict large cash payments and receipts, and a business expense paid in cash above the permitted limit can be disallowed. Your CA/CPA can tell you the current limits. A dated cash book with a description against each entry is what you will need if a cash expense or a cash deposit into the bank is ever questioned. Record [petty cash](/glossary/petty-cash) spends as they happen rather than in one lump at month-end.

items.question: What is the difference between gross profit and net profit on the dashboard?
items.answer: Gross profit is revenue minus cost of goods: what is left from sales after paying for the stock you sold. Net profit then subtracts the expenses recorded in the Expense Tracker, such as rent, salaries and electricity. A healthy gross profit with a weak net profit usually points to overheads, while a thin gross profit points to pricing or purchase costs.

items.question: Does the profit shown include GST?
items.answer: On the sales side, yes. Revenue is the total of each completed POS bill, including any GST charged on it, so for a GST-registered business the revenue and profit figures include output GST that you collect for the government. Cost of goods and expenses use whatever amounts you entered, with or without GST. For tax filing and returns, rely on your books or your CA/CPA's figures.

body.headline: What is a profit dashboard?
paragraphs: A **profit dashboard** is a one-screen view of what your business earned after costs over a chosen period. Instead of waiting for a year-end [profit and loss statement](/glossary/profit-and-loss-statement) from your accountant, you see five figures for today, the last 7 days, the last 30 days or any custom dates: revenue, cost of goods, [gross profit](/glossary/gross-profit), expenses and net profit. Two charts sit underneath, revenue by day and expenses by category, so you can see which days carry the business and where the money goes.

For a shop or restaurant owner, sales alone are misleading. A busy week can still lose money if ingredient costs rose or a large repair bill landed. Gross profit tells you whether your prices cover what you pay for stock; net profit tells you whether the business as a whole is paying for rent, staff and power. Watching both every week lets you act on a margin problem within days instead of discovering it when the month's books are closed.

A few details decide how far you can trust the figure. Only completed POS bills count, so cancelled bills never inflate revenue. Cost of goods uses each product's current cost price, so a product with no cost price saved adds nothing to it and makes gross profit look better than it is. Expenses count on the date you gave them in the Expense Tracker, so a large quarterly or annual bill lands in full on that day; judge such periods on a 30-day or custom range.

Record rent, salaries, bills and other spending in the Expense Tracker in the same browser.
Open the Profit Dashboard and tap Use workspace on the banner to include your POS sales and product costs.
Pick a range: Today, Last 7 days, Last 30 days, or Custom with your own from and to dates.
Read the five tiles from revenue down to net profit; the net profit figure turns red when the period made a loss.
Tap View table under Revenue by day for day-wise revenue and expenses, and use Expenses by category to find your biggest costs.

body.headline: What is a customer ledger, and why keep one?
paragraphs: A **customer ledger** is a separate account for each customer who buys on credit. Every time you hand over goods without collecting the full amount, their balance goes up; every time they pay, it comes down. In Indian shops this is the udhaar khata or bahi khata, the notebook behind the counter with a page for each family or regular buyer. Its job is simple: at any moment you should be able to say exactly who owes you how much, and since when, without flipping through months of handwriting.

Credit is how many kirana stores, medical shops, dairies and small wholesalers keep regular customers, but unrecorded udhaar is also where cash quietly leaks. A forgotten ₹200 here and ₹500 there add up over a year. Deciding a [credit limit](/glossary/credit-limit) for each regular customer, and checking their balance before you give more, stops one unpaid account from eating a month's margin. The total your customers owe is part of your [accounts receivable](/glossary/accounts-receivable), and your CA/CPA will ask for it when preparing your accounts. If you are GST-registered, a credit sale still needs its tax invoice or bill; the khata tracks who has paid, not the tax.

body.headline: What is a credit note?
paragraphs: A credit note is the document a seller issues to reduce what a customer owes on an invoice that has already gone out. It does not cancel or replace that invoice: the invoice stays in your books as issued, and the credit note sits beside it, quoting its number and recording how much comes off and why. This credit note generator builds that document: the invoice it adjusts, the reason, the items and tax being credited, and the total that comes off the customer's balance.

Under GST, a registered supplier issues a [credit note](/glossary/credit-note) when the taxable value or tax on an invoice turns out higher than it should be, when goods are returned, or when goods or services supplied are found deficient. You report it in your [GSTR-1](/glossary/gstr-1), which lowers your output tax for that period, and a GST-registered customer reduces the input tax credit they took on the original invoice. The law also sets a deadline after the financial year ends for declaring credit notes against that year's invoices, so raise them as returns happen rather than leaving them for a year-end clean-up.

The credit note lists 2 chairs at ₹2,500 with tax at the same 18% charged on the invoice: ₹5,000 plus ₹900 GST, a total of ₹5,900, against INV-0142 with the reason Return of goods. body.headline: What is a debit note?
paragraphs: A debit note is the buyer's formal claim against a supplier's bill. It names the bill, states the reason and values the adjustment line by line, so the supplier can check it and your books can show the reduced amount you owe. A buyer's debit note for a return is a commercial document: the GST adjustment happens when the supplier issues a matching [credit note](/glossary/credit-note) and reports it, after which you reduce the input tax credit you claimed. body.headline: What is a purchase order?
paragraphs: A purchase order, or PO, is the buyer's written order to a supplier: what you want, how many, at what agreed rate, with what tax, and by when. Once the supplier accepts it, both sides work from the same written list. A PO is not a tax invoice and carries no GST of its own; GST is charged on the supplier's bill. This purchase order generator gives you a numbered PO, ready to sign, in a couple of minutes, for anything from a weekly vegetable order to a shop fit-out.

The real value shows when the goods arrive. Your staff check the delivery against the PO and note what was received on a goods receipt note; when the supplier's bill comes, you match bill, PO and receipt before paying. That [three-way match](/glossary/three-way-match) catches short supply, substituted brands and rates that crept up since the order. Open POs also tell you how much you have already committed to spend, which matters when cash is tight at month-end.

Put payment terms on the PO too, not only on the supplier's bill. If the supplier is a registered micro or small enterprise, the [MSME payment rules](/glossary/msme-45-day-payment-rule) cap agreed credit at 45 days, and paying later can attract interest under that law. Restaurants ordering weekly from the same vendors, shops restocking before festivals and clinics buying consumables in bulk all gain from a PO trail where these terms are written down.

items.question: What is a chart of accounts?
items.answer: The master list of every account your business records money against — assets, liabilities, equity, income and expenses. Every journal entry posts to accounts from this list.

items.question: What do the account codes mean?
items.answer: A common convention: 1000s for assets, 2000s liabilities, 3000s equity, 4000s income, 5000s expenses. Numbering leaves gaps so you can slot new accounts in later.

items.question: Does this connect to the other bookkeeping tools?
items.answer: Yes — the Journal Entry, General Ledger and Trial Balance tools on this site read this same chart automatically, all inside your browser.

items.question: How many accounts should a small business chart of accounts have?
items.answer: Enough to answer the questions you actually ask, and no more. Many small shops, restaurants and clinics manage with roughly 20 to 40 accounts. The general template here starts with 18, and the industry templates carry between 21 and 24. Add an account only when you need that number on its own, such as Packaging Material for a retail store; too many accounts slow down every entry.

items.question: Can I change an account code to match my accountant's or Tally's numbering?
items.answer: There is no edit button for an existing account. Delete it and add it again with the code and name your accountant uses. Codes are free text, and the list sorts them numerically. Do this before you post journal entries, because postings to a deleted account lose their link to it and show as a deleted account in the journal.

items.question: What is the difference between a chart of accounts and a general ledger?
items.answer: The chart of accounts is the list of accounts, each with a code, a name and a type. The general ledger is the record of what has been posted to each of those accounts, with a running balance. On this site you build the list here, post transactions in the Journal Entry tool, and the General Ledger tool shows each account's postings.

items.question: Will loading an industry template delete my journal entries?
items.answer: No. Loading a template replaces only the account list, and only after you confirm. Your journal entries stay as they are. Postings to accounts the new template also has, such as Cash in Hand or Sales Revenue, stay linked. Postings to accounts you added yourself, or to ones the template drops, such as Inventory in the Services template, show as a deleted account. Template accounts are matched by code, so postings to one template's 1210 account show under the next template's 1210.

body.headline: What is a chart of accounts used for?
paragraphs: A chart of accounts decides where every rupee is sorted before it reaches your [profit and loss statement](/glossary/profit-and-loss-statement) and [balance sheet](/glossary/balance-sheet). If rent, electricity and staff salaries all land in one Expenses account, you cannot tell which cost is rising. A good chart of accounts for a small business is short enough to use every day, yet detailed enough to answer the questions you ask most: how much went on purchases, what customers still owe and how much GST you owe.

Businesses that keep books in Tally know these accounts as ledgers, grouped under heads such as Current Assets, Sundry Debtors, Duties & Taxes and Indirect Expenses. The idea is the same: each account belongs to exactly one group, and the groups roll up into your final accounts. When your CA/CPA prepares the year-end statements or works on a tax audit, a clean and consistent account list makes the job faster and cuts down the questions sent back to you.

The chart is also where good bookkeeping habits start. Tax collected on sales goes into GST Payable, not Sales Revenue. Money the owner takes home goes into Owner's Drawings, not Salaries & Wages. A cash deposit into the bank is a move between two asset accounts, not income. Set these accounts up correctly once, and every journal entry, ledger and trial balance built on them follows the same rules.

items.question: How do debits and credits work?
items.answer: Every transaction touches at least two accounts, and total debits must equal total credits. Paying ₹10,000 rent by bank: debit Rent Expense ₹10,000, credit Bank ₹10,000. The tool blocks unbalanced entries.

items.answer: No. You type the amounts yourself. In those entries GST paid on purchases is debited to the same GST Payable account, so its balance is the net of tax collected and input credit.

body.headline: What is a journal entry in double-entry bookkeeping?
paragraphs: A journal entry is the first record of a business transaction: the date, the accounts it touches, the amount on the debit side, the amount on the credit side and a narration saying what happened. In [double-entry bookkeeping](/glossary/double-entry-bookkeeping) the journal is called the book of original entry, because everything else, from account ledgers to the trial balance and final accounts, is built from it. Read in date order, it is the day-by-day history of your business.

If you have used Tally, you have already made journal entries, even if the screen called them payment, receipt, contra, sales or purchase vouchers. Each of those is a debit-and-credit record underneath. Your CA/CPA, and the auditor in a [tax audit](/glossary/tax-audit), trace figures in the final accounts back to these vouchers, so an entry with a clear narration and a bill or cheque reference saves time and follow-up questions at year end.

Many errors in small-business books come from picking the wrong account rather than from wrong arithmetic. GST collected gets credited to sales, the owner's withdrawals get booked as salary, and a cash deposit into the bank is recorded as income. Each of those entries balances perfectly and is still wrong. Choosing accounts deliberately, and asking what an entry does to profit and to what you owe, matters more than speed.

items.question: Where does the ledger data come from?
items.answer: From the Journal Entry tool on this site. Every posted entry appears in the ledger of each account it touches — no re-typing.

items.question: What does the Dr/Cr balance mean?
items.answer: Asset and expense accounts normally carry debit (Dr) balances; liability, equity and income accounts carry credit (Cr) balances. The ledger shows the running balance on the account's normal side.

items.question: Can I export a ledger?
items.answer: Yes — export any account's ledger as CSV with dates, narrations, debits, credits and the running balance.

items.question: What is the difference between a journal and a ledger?
items.answer: The journal records each transaction once, in date order, with all its debit and credit lines together. The ledger takes those same lines and sorts them by account, adding a running balance. Here you write only in the Journal Entry tool; the ledger is read-only and built from it, so the two can never disagree.

items.question: How do I enter opening balances in the general ledger?
items.answer: There is no separate opening balance field. Post one journal entry dated the first day of your financial year, or the day you start using the tool: debit each asset account with its opening balance, credit each liability account with its balance, and put the difference to Owner's Capital so the entry balances. Each account's ledger then starts from that figure.

items.question: Can I view a ledger for one month or a date range?
items.answer: Not inside the tool. It shows every posting to the chosen account from the first entry onward. To look at one month, export the ledger as CSV and filter the Date column in Excel or Google Sheets. The running balance on each row is still correct, because it is calculated from the start of the journal.

items.question: Why does my cash or bank ledger show a Cr balance?
items.answer: It means more has been credited to the account than debited, so the balance has gone below zero. Cash cannot really be negative, so look for a missed receipt, an unrecorded sale or a payment posted twice. For the bank account, a Cr balance may be a genuine overdraft; compare it with your bank statement to be sure.

body.headline: What is a general ledger?
paragraphs: A general ledger is the account-by-account record that sits behind your financial statements. The journal lists transactions in date order; the ledger regroups the same postings by account, so you can open Bank Account, Sales Revenue or Rent Expense and see every debit, every credit and the balance after each one. The closing balances of all the ledgers make up the [trial balance](/glossary/trial-balance), which in turn feeds the profit and loss statement and balance sheet.

In India, accountants often say ledger when they mean a single account: a party ledger for a supplier, the bank ledger, the GST ledger. Tally works the same way. When your CA/CPA prepares final accounts or checks figures for a tax audit, ledger extracts answer specific questions: why rent went up, whether a supplier's balance agrees with their [statement of account](/glossary/statement-of-account), and whether the GST booked matches what was paid.

A running balance is also the quickest way to catch mistakes. A cash account that goes negative, a supplier account showing a debit balance, or an expense that doubles in one month usually means something was posted to the wrong account or on the wrong side. Spotting it in the ledger during the year is far easier than unpicking it after the books are closed.

items.question: Why don't my bank and book balances match?
items.answer: Timing and omissions: cheques you issued that haven't cleared, deposits the bank hasn't credited yet, bank charges and interest you haven't recorded. Each is a reconciling item.

items.question: How often should I reconcile?
items.answer: Monthly at minimum, when the bank statement arrives. Busy businesses reconcile weekly — the sooner you catch an error or a missing entry, the easier it is to fix.

items.question: What if a difference remains after adjusting?
items.answer: Check for transposed digits (a difference divisible by 9 is a classic sign), duplicated entries, or a transaction recorded on the wrong side. The tool shows the residual difference live as you add items.

items.question: What is the difference between a deposit in transit and an outstanding cheque?
items.answer: A deposit in transit is money you have recorded as banked but the bank has not credited yet, such as a cheque deposited on the last day of the month. It is added to the bank balance. An outstanding cheque is one you have issued and recorded, but the payee has not presented or the bank has not cleared. It is subtracted from the bank balance.

items.question: Should a BRS start from the bank balance or the book balance?
items.answer: Either works. Textbook formats usually start from one balance and adjust towards the other. This tool adjusts both: the bank balance for deposits in transit and outstanding cheques, and the book balance for bank credits and charges you have not recorded yet. The test is the same either way: the two adjusted balances must be equal.

items.question: Can I upload my bank statement to reconcile automatically?
items.answer: No. This tool does not import statement files. You type in the two closing balances and each reconciling item yourself, which is quick for a typical small-business month with a handful of differences. For a busy account, match the statement against your books in a spreadsheet first, then enter only the unmatched items here.

items.question: Can I keep a separate reconciliation for each month?
items.answer: The tool holds one reconciliation at a time. Before you start the next month, click Print / PDF or Export CSV to keep a copy of the current one. Then enter the new closing balances, delete the items that have since cleared, and leave in place any cheque still outstanding or deposit still in transit.

body.headline: What is a bank reconciliation statement (BRS)?
paragraphs: A bank reconciliation statement, or BRS, explains why the bank balance in your [cash book](/tools/cash-book) differs from the balance on your bank statement on the same date. It lists the items only one side has recorded so far and adjusts for them until both figures agree. When they do, you know every rupee in the account is accounted for in your books, and anything left over points to an error or a missing entry.

In India the BRS is a routine part of bookkeeping and audit work, and auditors commonly ask for one for each bank account as at 31 March, along with the bank statements. For shops and restaurants, many gaps now come less from cheques and more from card and payment-gateway settlements that reach the bank a day or more later, often as one lump sum net of [MDR](/glossary/mdr) or gateway fees.

This tool uses the adjusted-balance format. Instead of starting from one balance and working towards the other, it corrects both: the bank balance for items the bank has not processed yet, and the book balance for items the bank has processed but you have not recorded. If the two adjusted figures are equal, the account is reconciled. If not, whatever is left is the amount you still have to explain.

items.question: How is a trial balance different from a balance sheet?
items.answer: A trial balance lists every ledger account, including income and expenses, to check that debits equal credits. It is an internal working paper. A balance sheet is a final statement showing only assets, liabilities and equity, prepared after the year's income and expenses have been worked into profit and added to equity. The trial balance comes first and supplies the numbers for both final statements.

body.headline: What is a trial balance used for?
paragraphs: A trial balance is the checkpoint between day-to-day bookkeeping and the final accounts. Before anyone draws up a profit and loss account or a balance sheet, the closing balance of every ledger account is listed as on one date and the debit and credit columns are totalled. Accountants prepare one at each [month-end close](/glossary/month-end-close) and again at 31 March, when the year's books are finalised. It is a working paper for you and your CA/CPA, not a statement you file or send to customers.

Matching totals prove that debits equal credits; they do not prove the books are right. An entry left out altogether, posted twice, or posted to the wrong account will still balance, and so will two mistakes that cancel each other. Use the trial balance to catch arithmetic and posting errors quickly, then review the accounts themselves. Read down the list as well as across the totals: a balance sitting on an unusual side is often the first sign of a posting error.

In India your CA/CPA will usually ask for a trial balance before finalising accounts for the income tax return or a [tax audit](/glossary/tax-audit), and Tally users will know it as one of the standard reports. If your books are kept elsewhere, a trial balance in a standard format, exported as CSV, gives the CA/CPA the same starting point: every account, its net balance and the side it falls on. A suspense account still carrying a balance at year-end means something has not been sorted out.

body.headline: What is a profit and loss statement used for?
paragraphs: A profit and loss statement, also called an income statement or P&L, measures performance over a period, such as a month, a quarter or the April to March financial year, rather than the position on one date. It answers a single question: after paying for stock, rent, salaries and everything else, did the business make money in that period, and how much? The balance sheet is a photograph of one day; the P&L explains the months that led up to it.

Your CA/CPA uses the P&L to work out taxable business income for the income tax return, and banks read it alongside the balance sheet before sanctioning a loan or overdraft. For the owner, a monthly P&L is more useful than an annual one. It shows a falling [gross profit](/glossary/gross-profit) margin soon after supplier rates rise, or rent and salaries creeping up as a share of sales, while there is still time to change prices or cut costs.

Two habits keep an Indian P&L honest. Enter sales without the GST you charged, because that tax belongs to the government and only passes through your hands until you pay it with GSTR-3B. Enter purchases without GST too when you claim [input tax credit](/glossary/input-tax-credit) on them. A composition-scheme business is different: it cannot collect GST from customers or claim credit, so the GST on its purchases is part of their cost and the tax it pays on turnover is an expense.

body.headline: What does a balance sheet tell a small business owner?
paragraphs: A balance sheet answers "where do I stand today?" rather than "how did I do this month?". It is drawn up as of one date, most often 31 March, the last day of the Indian financial year, and sets everything the business owns against everything it owes. This balance sheet maker uses a simple single-column format: current and fixed assets add up to total assets, current and long-term liabilities add up to total liabilities, and equity is added to that to give total liabilities and equity.

Banks and NBFCs usually ask for a balance sheet, together with the profit and loss account, when you apply for a business loan, an overdraft or a [working capital](/glossary/working-capital) limit. Your CA/CPA prepares the final one at year-end for the income tax return or an audit. A balance sheet you build yourself during the year is still worth the effort: it shows early whether loans are growing faster than assets, whether stock is piling up, or whether losses are eating into the owner's capital.

For a GST-registered shop, a few lines need care. GST collected on sales but not yet paid to the government is a current liability, not income, so it belongs under GST payable. Unused input tax credit is usually shown as a current asset. Owner's capital is the money you put in, and [retained earnings](/glossary/retained-earnings) is the profit kept in the business over the years. For a proprietorship, many CAs/CPAs show both as one capital account: opening capital plus profit, minus drawings.

items.question: Why track cash flow separately from profit?

items.question: What goes in each section?

items.question: Why is my closing cash negative?
items.answer: A red closing figure means more cash went out than the opening balance plus everything that came in. Cash in hand cannot really go below zero, so usually an inflow is missing, such as a loan or capital introduced, the opening balance is wrong, or a payment has been entered twice. A bank overdraft is the one case where a negative balance can be genuine.

items.question: Is a cash flow statement the same as a cash book?
items.answer: No. A cash book records each cash transaction on its date with a running balance. A cash flow statement summarises a whole period, covers bank as well as cash, and groups the movements into operating, investing and financing activities. The cash book is the daily record; the cash flow statement is the summary you show a lender or review at the end of the period.

body.headline: What is a cash flow statement?
paragraphs: A cash flow statement records the actual movement of money into and out of the business over a period, sorted into operating, investing and financing activities. It starts with the cash and bank balance on the first day and ends with the balance on the last, and every rupee of difference is explained by a line in between. That makes it the easiest statement to check: the closing figure should match the cash you count plus your bank balance on that date, after reconciling it.

Several everyday transactions move cash without touching profit. Repaying the principal of a business loan empties the bank account but never appears as an expense. A new oven or fridge paid for in full reaches the P&L only slowly, as [depreciation](/glossary/depreciation). Money the owner withdraws for the household is not an expense either. Seeing these in one place explains why the bank balance can fall in months that the profit and loss account calls profitable.

Indian accounting standards (AS 3, or Ind AS 7 for companies that follow Ind AS) allow the operating section to be shown in two ways. The direct method lists cash received from customers and paid to suppliers and staff; the indirect method starts from net profit and adjusts for non-cash items and [working capital](/glossary/working-capital) changes. The starter lines in this tool follow the direct method, which is easier to fill from a cash book and bank passbook. Audited accounts often use the indirect method.

body.headline: What is a debtor statement used for?
paragraphs: A **customer statement**, also called a [statement of account](/glossary/statement-of-account) or debtor statement, lets a customer check your figures line by line instead of disputing a lump sum. In your books the customer is a debtor, so what you bill them sits in the Debit column, and what they pay or you allow back sits in Credit. Their accounts team keeps the mirror image: your invoices are credits in their account for you, and their payments are debits. When both sides list the same lines, the closing balances agree. When they do not, the statement shows exactly where the difference starts.

In India, statements do much of their work around 31 March, when auditors often ask businesses to confirm balances with major customers. Differences usually come from three places: a payment received but not yet entered, a credit note one side has missed, or [TDS](/glossary/tds) the customer deducted before paying you. TDS settles part of the invoice even though that money went to the government and not to your bank, so it needs its own line instead of being left as an unexplained gap. Ask the customer to confirm the closing balance in writing, and keep their reply with your year-end papers.

items.answer: The oldest. Collection odds fall sharply with age — industry studies put the expected recovery of a debt past 90 days well below face value. The 90+ column is your priority list.

items.question: How do overdue invoices affect my business?
items.answer: Money in the 30+ buckets is working capital you're lending interest-free while possibly paying for your own credit. Check the Payment Terms calculator to price early-payment discounts that pull cash in faster.

items.question: How are days overdue counted in the invoice aging report?
items.answer: From the due date you enter, not the invoice date. An invoice due today or later is Not yet due. After that, the days since the due date decide the bucket: 1–30, 31–60, 61–90 or 90+. An invoice due on 10 September is 37 days overdue on 17 October and appears in the 31–60 column. Invoices move into older buckets automatically as time passes.

items.question: What is the difference between an aging report and a customer statement?
items.answer: An aging report covers all your customers at once and groups what they owe by how overdue it is, so you can decide whom to chase first. A customer statement covers one customer and lists every invoice, payment and credit note with a running balance. Use the aging report to plan collections, then send each overdue customer a statement with your reminder.

items.question: Should I remove an invoice when the customer pays part of it?
items.answer: Remove it and add it back at the reduced amount. The report has no part-payment entry, so tap Paid / remove on the invoice and add it again with the balance still due and the original due date. Keeping the original due date means the remaining amount stays in the right bucket instead of looking freshly issued.

items.question: When should an old invoice be written off as a bad debt?
items.answer: There is no fixed day count. Most businesses review everything in the 90+ bucket with their accountant at year end and write off amounts where the customer has closed, cannot be traced or has refused to pay despite repeated reminders. Keep a record of the calls, messages and statements you sent, because it supports the decision if your auditor asks why a balance was written off.

body.headline: What is debtor aging analysis, and who uses it?
paragraphs: An **invoice aging report**, also called accounts receivable aging or debtor aging analysis, lists the money customers owe you and sorts it by how far past the due date each invoice is. Your sales figures show what you earned; the aging report shows how much of it is still sitting with customers. Owners use it to plan collection calls. Banks commonly ask for a debtors list by age when working out drawing power on a cash credit account. Your CA/CPA uses it at year end to judge which old balances may never come in and should be treated as [bad debt](/glossary/bad-debt).

For a GST-registered business, an unpaid invoice costs more than the wait. GST on a sale generally becomes payable based on the invoice date, not the date the customer pays, so you deposit the tax in your next return even if the customer has not paid you anything. A customer who pays 60 days late is borrowing that tax from you as well. Companies also have to show trade receivables by age in the notes to their balance sheet, so a running aging list makes the year-end close quicker. Tracking [days sales outstanding](/glossary/days-sales-outstanding) month on month tells you whether collections are improving.

body.headline: What is an accounts payable aging report used for?
paragraphs: An **accounts payable aging** report lists what you owe suppliers and sorts it by how long each bill has been past its due date, with a total for every age band and every supplier. It turns a pile of unpaid bills into figures you can act on: how much is overdue, how much is badly overdue, and to whom. Your accountant uses the same view to check trade payables at month end. It is also a quick first check when a supplier's statement does not match your books, because a very old unpaid bill is often one that was paid but never marked as paid.

In India, two rules make old payables costly. If you claim input tax credit on a purchase but do not pay the supplier within 180 days of the invoice date, you must [reverse that credit](/glossary/itc-reversal) with interest, and can claim it again once you pay. Udyam-registered micro and small manufacturers and service providers must be paid within the agreed credit period, capped at 45 days, or within 15 days if nothing is agreed in writing. Pay them later and the expense is deductible for income tax only in the year you actually pay. This [MSME 45-day rule](/glossary/msme-45-day-payment-rule) is why many CAs/CPAs ask for payables by age before the year closes.

items.question: What is budget variance?
items.answer: The difference between actual and budgeted amounts (actual − budget). For expense rows a positive variance means overspend; for revenue rows it means you beat the plan.

items.question: Which variances should I investigate?
items.answer: Big ones in money terms and big ones in percentage terms — a 2% miss on your largest cost can matter more than a 40% miss on a tiny one. Look at both columns.

items.question: How often should I review budget vs actual?
items.answer: Monthly is the standard rhythm — soon enough to correct course, spaced enough for real data. The tool keeps one sheet in this browser, so export a CSV before you overwrite a month's figures to keep a record.

items.question: Does Pull actuals from expenses use only the period I typed?
items.answer: No. The period box is a label only. Pulling actuals totals every expense saved in your Setu Expense Tracker for each matching category, whatever its date. If you record expenses across several months, check that month's total in the Expense Tracker and type the actual by hand, or the pulled figure will cover all months together.

items.question: How is variance percentage calculated?
items.answer: Variance % = (actual − budget) ÷ budget × 100. An electricity budget of ₹12,000 with an actual bill of ₹13,800 gives ₹1,800 ÷ ₹12,000 × 100 = 15.0%, shown in red because it is an expense row. When a row has no budget, the percentage cannot be calculated and shows a dash, though the rupee variance still appears.

items.question: Can I track revenue and expenses on the same sheet?
items.answer: Yes. Set each row's Type to Revenue or Expense. The colour logic flips for revenue rows: actual above budget shows green and below shows red, while for expense rows it is the other way round. Rows added with Add row, and new categories brought in by pulling actuals, start as Expense, so switch the type for any extra income line such as catering or online orders.

items.question: Can I keep budgets for several months in the tool?
items.answer: The tool holds one sheet at a time. A simple routine is to export the CSV at month end, then update the period label and figures for the next month. The file is always named budget-vs-actual.csv and does not include the period label, so rename it with the month to build a month-by-month record you can compare in Excel or Google Sheets.

body.headline: What is a budget vs actual report?
paragraphs: A **budget vs actual** report puts your plan for a period next to what really happened, line by line, and shows the gap in rupees and in percent. Each line is a category such as sales, rent, salaries or marketing. It is the simplest form of [budget variance analysis](/glossary/budget-variance) and the core of monthly [management accounts](/glossary/management-accounts). You do not need a full accounting system to run one, only a budget figure and a total from your books for each line.

Most small businesses set a rough monthly budget for a few big lines, such as staff, rent, raw material, power and marketing, and lose sight of it by the third week. Reviewing budget against actual every month catches drift early: an electricity bill that has risen three months running, a marketing spend that overran without extra sales, or a sales shortfall that will squeeze next month's cash. Lenders reviewing a working capital limit also tend to compare your projections with actual results, so the monthly habit saves a scramble later.

Suppose your July budget had sales of ₹5,00,000 and marketing of ₹20,000, and the actuals came in at ₹4,60,000 and ₹25,000. The sales variance is ₹4,60,000 − ₹5,00,000 = −₹40,000, or −8.0%, shown in red because revenue fell short. The marketing variance is ₹25,000 − ₹20,000 = +₹5,000, or +25.0%, also red because spending went over. Rent budgeted at ₹40,000 and paid at ₹40,000 shows zero variance in grey.

items: Name rows exactly as the Expense Tracker categories, such as Rent, Salaries or Electricity, with the same capitalisation, so pulled actuals land on the right row; a row renamed Shop rent gets a separate Rent row added instead

items.question: What is ABC analysis?
items.answer: An inventory method based on the Pareto principle: class A items are the vital few (~80% of consumption value), B the middle (~15%), C the trivial many (~5%). Each class gets a matching level of control.

items.question: How are items classified?
items.answer: Rank items by annual consumption value (annual quantity × unit cost), take the cumulative percentage of total value, and cut at 80% (A), 95% (B) and beyond (C) — exactly what this tool automates.

items.question: How should I treat each class?
items.answer: A: tight control — frequent counts, careful reorder points, negotiated pricing. B: moderate, periodic review. C: simple rules and bulk orders. Pair with our Stock Reorder Point calculator for the A items.

items.question: Is the ABC analysis tool free to use?
items.answer: Yes. It is free, needs no signup and has no fixed limit on the number of items. Your item list saves automatically in this browser, so it is still there when you come back on the same device. Clearing browser data removes it, and a private window forgets it once closed, so export a CSV if you want a permanent copy.

items.question: Should I use cost price or selling price for ABC analysis?
items.answer: Use cost price. ABC analysis measures how much money you spend to keep each item in stock, so annual quantity multiplied by purchase cost is the standard basis. Selling price would inflate high-margin items and hide costly low-margin ones. When you pull products from a Setu workspace, the tool uses each product's cost price and falls back to the selling price only when no cost price is saved.

items.question: What is the difference between ABC analysis and XYZ or FSN analysis?
items.answer: ABC analysis groups items by money value. XYZ analysis groups them by how steady their demand is, and FSN analysis by how fast they move: fast, slow or non-moving. They answer different questions, so many businesses combine them, for example by watching an A item with erratic demand more closely. This tool performs the ABC classification only.

items.question: Can I do ABC analysis on my phone?
items.answer: Yes. The tool runs in a phone browser, and the item table, ranking table and Pareto chart scroll sideways on small screens, while the class cards and pie chart stack to fit. For a long item list, typing on a laptop is quicker, and the list you save stays only in the browser you used, so pick one device for the analysis.

body.headline: What is ABC inventory classification?
paragraphs: **ABC analysis** sorts your stock list by how much money each item consumes in a year, so you know where to spend counting and ordering effort. For every item you multiply the quantity used or sold in a year by its unit cost, rank the results from highest to lowest, and tag each item A, B or C. The output is a ranked table showing usage value, share of the total, a running cumulative percentage and the class. It is an internal management report, not a statutory one, so you can run it as often as your buying cycle needs.

In an Indian shop, pharmacy, hardware store or restaurant kitchen, most of the cash locked in stock usually sits in a short list of items. Those are the lines where a stockout costs a sale, where a few rupees off the purchase rate adds up over a year, and where a counting mistake distorts your [closing stock](/glossary/closing-stock) at year end. ABC analysis puts that short list in front of you, so you can count A items more often, hold [safety stock](/glossary/safety-stock) for them, and buy C items in bulk without much thought.

The inputs are figures you already have. Annual quantity can come from last year's sales report, your purchase register or a Tally stock summary. Unit cost should be what you pay for the item, not what you sell it for, because the aim is to measure money spent on keeping stock. If you sell seasonal goods such as festival stock or school supplies, use the last twelve months rather than one month, or a slow season will push important items down into class C.

body.text: ABC analysis ranks by **usage value**, annual quantity × unit cost, not by how many units move. items.question: How does the scoring work?
items.answer: You score each vendor from 1 to 10 on every criterion. The tool multiplies each score by that criterion's weight, divides the total by the sum of the weights and shows the result out of 100, so the weights only need to be right relative to each other. Change a weight or a score and the ranking updates instantly.

items.question: What weights should I use?
items.answer: Match them to what hurts most when it goes wrong. Perishable goods? Weight delivery high. Tight cash? Weight credit terms. Customer-facing quality? Weight quality. The starting weights (Price 30, Quality 25, Delivery reliability 20, Credit terms 15, Support 10) are a sensible place to begin for retail buying.

items.question: Why not just pick the cheapest quote?
items.answer: The cheapest vendor who delivers late or supplies poor quality costs more in stockouts, returns and lost customers. A weighted score makes those trade-offs explicit instead of gut-feel.

items.question: Do the criteria weights have to add up to 100?
items.answer: No. The score divides the weighted total by the sum of all weights, so weights that total 80 or 120 rank vendors the same way as the same weights scaled to 100. The total weight indicator turns green at exactly 100 and amber otherwise, because 100 lets each weight read as a percentage.

items.question: How many vendors and criteria can I compare?
items.answer: Add as many vendors and criteria as you need; the table scrolls sideways when it gets wide, which also keeps it usable on a phone. A comparison needs at least two vendors and one criterion, so the remove button is disabled below that. Note that Load sample criteria replaces your current rows, and their scores, with the ten-criterion set.

items.question: What happens if I leave a vendor's score blank?
items.answer: A blank score counts as zero, so that vendor is treated as the worst possible on that criterion and its score drops. If you are missing a figure for one vendor, find it out or enter a cautious estimate. If no vendor can be scored on a criterion, delete the row or set its weight to zero, otherwise every score is dragged down and harder to compare with your next review.

items.question: Can I use this as a supplier scorecard for existing suppliers?
items.answer: Yes. Rate your current suppliers on the same criteria every quarter using real records such as late deliveries, rejected lots and price changes, and export a CSV each time. Comparing the exported scores over time shows which supplier is slipping before it hurts your stock. The tool holds one comparison at a time, so export before you reuse it.

body.headline: What is a vendor comparison matrix?
paragraphs: A **vendor comparison** matrix, also called a supplier scorecard or weighted decision matrix, lists the suppliers you are considering as columns and the things you care about as rows: price, quality, delivery reliability, credit terms and support. Each supplier gets a score on each row, each row carries a weight, and the weighted total ranks them. The result is one sheet that shows why a supplier was chosen, instead of a decision made from memory of the last phone call.

For a restaurant buying oil and dairy, a pharmacy choosing a distributor or a shop switching wholesalers, the cheapest rate card rarely tells the full story. Thirty days of credit instead of cash on delivery changes your [working capital](/glossary/working-capital). A supplier who issues correct tax invoices with your [GSTIN](/glossary/gstin) and files GST returns on time keeps your input tax credit flowing, while a distributor who misses delivery days forces emergency buying at retail rates. Writing these trade-offs down also gives you an answer when a partner, auditor or CA/CPA asks why a costlier vendor was approved.

The tool multiplies each score by its criterion weight, adds the results, divides by the total weight and multiplies by 10, giving a score out of 100. With the starting weights of Price 30, Quality 25, Delivery reliability 20, Credit terms 15 and Support 10, Vendor A scores 9, 6, 6, 8 and 5: 270 + 150 + 120 + 120 + 50 = 710, and 710 ÷ 100 × 10 = 71. Vendor B scores 6, 9, 9, 5 and 8: 180 + 225 + 180 + 75 + 80 = 740, or 74. B ranks first even though A has the better price.

steps: Rename Vendor A, Vendor B and Vendor C to your real suppliers, or tap Add vendor for more. If you have allowed workspace access and keep a Supplier Book, Load suppliers fills the vendor list from it. This replaces the current vendors, so do it before you start scoring.
Type what you are buying in the item box, for example cooking oil 15 L tins, monthly.

Review the criteria and weights. Rename or delete rows, tap Add criterion for your own, or tap Load sample criteria for a ten-row set that adds lead time, warranty, MOQ, shipping cost and GST compliance.
Score every vendor from 1 to 10 on each criterion, where 10 is best. For price, give the cheapest quote the highest score.
Read the Ranking card: each vendor gets a weighted score out of 100 and the leader is tagged Best value.
Tap Export CSV to save the criteria, weights, scores and final scores for your purchase file.

body.headline: What to score when comparing suppliers
items: Landed price per unit, including transport and loading charges, not just the rate on the quotation
Credit period, and whether the supplier charges interest or stops credit when you pay late
Delivery reliability over your last few orders, not the promise made in the sales meeting
Quality consistency, such as rejected or short-supplied quantity per delivery
GST compliance: correct tax invoices with your GSTIN and timely return filing, so your input tax credit is not held up
Minimum order quantity and lead time, which decide how much stock and cash you have to hold

hero.headline: Supplier Ledger
hero.subheadline: What you owe every supplier — credit bills, payments made and running balances in one place.

items.question: What is a supplier ledger?
items.answer: A running account for each supplier you buy from on credit. Bills increase what you owe them, payments reduce it, and the balance tells you exactly how much is still payable — the creditor side of your books, the mirror image of a customer udhaar khata.

items.question: Do I need to enter purchases twice?
items.answer: No. Any purchase recorded in the Setu Purchase Register with payment mode Credit appears in the supplier's ledger automatically. Purchases paid by Cash, UPI, Card or Bank transfer were settled on the spot, so they are not added as bills.

items.question: How are payments matched to bills?
items.answer: Pick a bill under Against bill to pay that bill specifically, or leave it on Oldest bills first and the payment settles the supplier's oldest unpaid bills first. If you pay more than you owe, the extra shows as an advance with that supplier.

items.question: How does it work with the Accounts Payable Aging report?
items.answer: Both use the same numbers. Pull from Purchase Register in the aging report brings in only credit bills that are still unpaid, and tapping Mark paid there records the payment in this ledger, so the bill never comes back.

items.question: Can I enter balances from my old books?
items.answer: Yes. Choose Bill / opening balance, enter the amount you owed the supplier on the day you started, and add a note such as old balance. Payments you record afterwards settle it like any other bill.

items.question: Where is my data stored?
items.answer: In your browser on your device, inside your Setu business workspace — the same one the Browser Based POS, Supplier Book and Purchase Register use. Nothing is uploaded; export a CSV backup any time.

body.headline: What is a supplier ledger (creditors ledger)?
paragraphs: A **supplier ledger**, also called a creditors ledger or accounts payable ledger, keeps one running account per supplier. Every bill you receive on credit increases what you owe, every payment you make reduces it, and the balance is the amount still payable. It is the mirror image of a [customer ledger](/tools/customer-ledger): there you track who owes you, here you track whom you owe.

body.headline: How to use the free supplier ledger
steps: Record purchases in the Purchase Register and choose Credit as the payment mode when you have not paid yet.
Open the Supplier Ledger and pick the supplier — their credit bills are already listed with the amount due.
When you pay, choose Payment made, pick the bill or leave Oldest bills first, choose how you paid and tap Record payment.
Use Bill / opening balance for amounts owed from before you started, or bills you did not record in the register.
Check the Accounts Payable Aging report to see which unpaid bills are getting old.

body.headline: Pay the oldest bills first
body.text: Suppliers usually apply payments to their oldest invoices, and this ledger settles an unlinked payment the same way, so your balance matches theirs. If a supplier asks you to clear a specific bill, pick it under Against bill when you record the payment. Check the [Accounts Payable Aging](/tools/accounts-payable-aging) report every week so no credit bill slips past its due date.
